newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Handelsbanken tops bids for bank.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Handelsbanken tops bids for bank.

text.p: Swedish high street bank Svenska Handelsbanken on Thursday launched a cash bid for the nation's biggest mortgage lender, Stadshypotek AB, topping a rival offer by Skandia Insurance Co.
The 22.9 billion crown ($3.36 billion) bid appeared fairly certain to go through after winning approval from the Swedish government, which is auctioning its 34 percent stake.
"The state has promised to accept the offer for its 34 percent, provided that any no better bids are received before the end of the offer period," a Handelsbanken statement said.

Topping Skandia's offer, which valued the mortgage bank at 20.6 billion crowns ($3.02 billion), Handelsbanken said it would pay 190 crowns for each Stadshypotek A-series share and 180 crowns for B-series shares.
Stadshypotek shares closed six crowns higher at 188 crowns. Handelsbanken shares closed 7.5 crowns higher at 196 and Skandia rose four to 190 crowns.
Handelsbanken chairman Arne Martensson told a news conference the bank would pay cash for Stadshypotek out of a 25 billion crown surplus the bank holds.
"We will use this cash surplus to fund the bid. You could say we're borrowing from ourselves," he said.
Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink told reporters in Dublin that Handelsbanken had made the best bid for Stadshypotek since the auction opened on December 2.
"Svenska Handelsbanken has put forward the best offer and is prepared to pay cash for the state's shares," he said.
"The state accepts (the) bid but reserves the right to accept a higher bid. Given the sale processes carried out by the finance ministry, however, no higher bids are expected."
Rival suitor Skandia said it had no plans to increase its offer for Stadshypotek which is Sweden's largest mortgage lender, with one third of the market.
"Raising the bid is not on the agenda ... we would not dream of changing it," Skandia board chairman Sven Soderberg told Reuters.
The announcement was welcomed by the market, which pushed the shares of all three institutions higher.
"The bid is good for Stadshypotek shareholders as it offers a premium," said James Capel analyst Frederik Myren.
"But although the bid might be structurally right for Handelsbanken, it will be difficult for the bank to defend the 40 percent mortgage banking share it will get."
Matteus analyst Bjorn Germer said the deal would be good for Sweden's financial sector.
"When a bank, like Handelsbanken, shows (through the bid) that it focuses on core banking activities, the market will interpret it favourably," Germer said.
"In addition, investors will get a lot of money which is likely to be reinvested in the finance sector."
The announcement ended three weeks of speculation over Stadshypotek since the government unveiled plans to auction its 34 percent stake.

Two days after the government unveiled its plans, Skandia and Stadshypotek announced a proposal to merge. However, the proposal was fiercely criticised by Asbrink who blasted Stadshypotek, saying he had no confidence in its board.
Asbrink said the government would push ahead with its plans to auction Stadshypotek and not be deterred by the merger proposal that seemed designed to bypass the auction process.

Handelsbanken, which posted a 19 percent lift in profit after credit losses of 4.52 billion crowns in the first nine months of 1996, had been tipped by some market players as the best suitor for Stadshypotek in economic terms and as the best placed to take on major mortgage interests. ($1=6.810 Swedish Crown)
